method: A Lambert conformal conic map unrolls a cone that cuts the ellipsoid along two standard parallels, where the scale is exactly 1 and the map is at true scale; between them it is slightly small and outside them it grows. With the semi-major axis a, first eccentricity e, and the functions m(phi) = cos phi / sqrt(1 - e^2 sin^2 phi) and t(phi) = tan(pi/4 - phi/2) / ((1 - e sin phi) / (1 + e sin phi))^(e/2), the page computes the cone constant n = ln(m1 / m2) / ln(t1 / t2) for two parallels, or n = sin phi1 when the two are equal (the single-parallel form), then F = m1 / (n t1^n) and the radius rho = a F t^n. A point lands at x = rho sin(n dlambda) and y = rho0 - rho cos(n dlambda) east and north of the origin, where dlambda is the longitude measured from the central meridian, wrapped into -180 to 180 degrees, and rho0 is rho at the latitude of origin; the false easting and northing are then added, so the northing of the latitude of origin is the false northing. The scale factor is k = n rho / (a m), exactly 1 on each standard parallel, below 1 between them and above 1 outside; grid convergence is n dlambda, the angle between grid north and true north, positive east of the central meridian in a northern cone and negative there in a southern one, so a point on the central meridian has zero convergence and only a northing. Conformality is exact: angles and small shapes are preserved at every point even though scale varies, which is why the projection carries aeronautical charts and many State Plane zones. Scale grows steeply away from the parallels: the default Continental US grid (33 and 45 degrees north, origin 39 degrees north on 96 degrees west, WGS 84) puts Washington DC at 1,624,568.7 m east and 157,935.0 m north with k = 0.994546 and convergence 11.9572 degrees, while a point on either parallel returns k = 1 and the antimeridian cases reduce to a pure northing. The inverse solves rho from the grid, recovers t = (rho / (a F))^(1/n), iterates latitude from t in the usual way and reads longitude from theta / n, keeping the sign of rho for southern cones so that eastings still increase eastwards. Refused rather than guessed: a point exactly on either pole (the cone apex has no longitude and the opposite pole has no image), standard parallels on the equator, parallels that straddle it, a latitude of origin in the opposite hemisphere, any latitude or longitude outside its range, and a grid position exactly at the apex. Offered are WGS 84, GRS 80, Clarke 1866 and a mean-radius sphere; no datum shift, no scale factor k0, no Michigan variant, no grid rotation and no false-origin azimuth are modelled, and the page does not draw the map. Pure local arithmetic: no upload, storage or network access.
